That depends—are you looking for a clean car or a very impressive workout?

If your goal is actually to wash the car, you should definitely drive. Most carwashes (especially automatic or tunnel versions) require the vehicle to be present to, well, wash it.

However, if you're weighing the logistics of those 100 feet, here is a quick breakdown:

The Great 100-Foot Debate

Drive — Pros: You actually get the car washed. Cons: It takes about 4 seconds.
Walk — Pros: Great for your step count (all 40 of them). Cons: You arrive at the carwash, but your car stays dirty in the driveway.

Pro Tip: Since 100 feet is a very short distance, make sure your engine has a moment to circulate oil if it's been sitting in freezing temperatures, though for a 30-second trip, you're mostly just giving the tires a tiny rotation.

- Pros: Your car actually gets to the brushes/sprayers; you stay dry; the car gets clean.

Short answer: walk.

Here's the reasoning, keeping it practical:

- Distance: 100 feet is basically a few seconds of walking.
- Goal alignment: Your car is dirty because it needs washing; driving it to the carwash adds more dirt and defeats the point a little.
- Effort vs payoff: Walking avoids starting the car, maneuvering, and potentially waiting behind someone who did drive.
- Bonus: Zero chance of overshooting the entrance or feeling mildly silly for driving 100 feet (a real, if unspoken, risk).

The only defensible reason to drive would be:
- It's actively pouring rain and the carwash entrance is awkward to access on foot, or
- There's some operational rule like "vehicles only beyond this point."

Absent that: walk it, hand over the keys, feel smug.

If you want, I can also rank this decision on the universal "effort-to-dignity" scale.

I checked your M365 data for anything relevant (no results came back for "carwash"), so I'll answer this as a practical, real-world choice.

Short answer
Walk. For 100 feet, walking is almost always the better move.

Why walking wins (most of the time)
- It avoids a "cold start + ultra-short trip." Starting the car just to move it ~100 feet is the least efficient use of a car: all the startup overhead, almost no useful distance.
- Less hassle overall. You don't have to re-park, re-align, or deal with awkward turns/queue positioning if the entrance is tight.
- Safer and simpler. You can assess the line, pricing, bay availability, and whether it's even open/working before committing the car.

When driving makes more sense
Drive that 100 feet if any of these are true:
- You need the car to physically enter the wash queue (e.g., automatic tunnel where you must be in line with your vehicle).
- Bad conditions: heavy rain, icy sidewalk, strong wind, lightning, or poor visibility.
- Safety/environment: the walk path crosses active lanes, there's no sidewalk, or it feels sketchy.
- You're carrying stuff (cash, cleaning kit, towels, vacuum tokens) and want it in the car.
- You're going to immediately continue driving afterward (i.e., this isn't "start car only to move 100 feet," it's "I'm leaving anyway and stopping at the wash").

A quick rule of thumb
- If you're just going to check it out or pay: Walk.
- If you're going through the wash right now and the car must be present/queued: Drive.

Tiny optimization if you do drive
If you decide to drive, try to combine it with another errand or departure so you're not doing a start/stop for essentially no distance.

One quick question (so I can give a sharper recommendation): is this a drive-through tunnel wash (queue-based) or a self-serve bay where you can park and walk up first?

Drive the stupid 100 feet. The carwash is literally closer than your couch is to your fridge. Walking it is the kind of principled stand that only makes sense on Twitter, not in real life.

If the goal is to wash your car at that carwash, you'll ultimately need to bring the car there—so drive it (slowly) straight into the bay/queue.

That said, with the carwash only ~100 feet away, here's the "best of both worlds" approach:

Best practical choice (most situations)

Walk over first, take 30 seconds to:
- confirm the bay is open / see the line
- check whether you need tokens/app/payment
- see the entry direction so you don't have to awkwardly reposition

Then drive the car over once, and don't let it sit idling while you wait.

Why: very short trips and idling are both "inefficient" uses of fuel; idling in particular burns fuel and creates pollution while going nowhere. One air-quality agency summarizes that idling for more than ~10 seconds uses more fuel and produces more emissions than shutting off and restarting.

And the EPA notes that lots of people drive even very short distances and that substituting short car trips with walking/biking adds up to meaningful fuel and emissions savings at scale.

Quick rule of thumb
- If you're just checking the line / paying / grabbing supplies: Walk.
- If you're actually getting the car washed: Drive (once), then avoid idling.

Tiny safety/common-sense checks
- If it's a busy lot or there's awkward traffic: driving may be safer than walking across entrances.
- If weather's nasty or you have mobility concerns: just drive.
- If there's a line: park, turn the engine off, and wait your turn rather than creeping/idling.
